title: Congratulations! Your Child Belongs in Algebra
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman praises Fairfax County Public Schools for automatically enrolling more 8th graders in Algebra I Honors, but argues their parent communications undermined the initiative by focusing on risk and opt-out rather than celebrating student capability. He brings in communications expert Michelle Lerner to draft a model letter that personalizes the message, leads with congratulations, and frames acceleration as an opportunity rather than a burden. The revised letter centers the student by name, explains the value of early algebra for future coursework, and removes barriers to enrollment. The article demonstrates that even well-designed equity policies can be weakened by poor messaging, and that school districts owe families communication that matches the ambition of their programs. Aldeman's broader point is that messaging algebra acceleration as a default good—rather than a risky experiment—sends a fundamentally different signal about what schools believe students can do.
points: Automatic enrollment policies require equally confident communications: when Fairfax enrolled more students in Algebra by default, their letters still emphasized opt-out pathways over celebrating the placement, effectively undercutting the equity intent of the policy.

Personalization in school communications matters: a letter that addresses a child by name and references their specific academic success is far more likely to be taken seriously than a generic district-wide announcement.

The framing of a policy shapes how families receive it: leading with 'Congratulations' rather than 'Here are your options to drop out' communicates what the school actually believes about the student's potential.
High-quality acceleration communication should excite about the standard: if schools aren't enthusiastic about students taking Algebra in 8th grade, they can't expect families to be.
Equity in course-taking depends on both enrollment policy AND how that policy is explained: getting students into the course is only half the work.
quotes: They felt a bit impersonal and overly focused on risks without emphasizing the potential benefits to students. There's a tension between laying out logistics while also expressing a belief that the student is being selected for acceleration because they're likely to be successful.

Congratulations! Based on [Student First Name]'s success in Advanced Math, [Student First Name] will be enrolled in Algebra 1 Honors next year. This is a high school-level class that moves at an accelerated pace and will be included on [Student First Name]'s high school transcript and GPA.
It's possible for districts to both create and implement great policies and to communicate about them effectively, which families want.
The original letter clearly signaled the ways a student could opt out, but didn't clearly explain the benefits.

At Fairfax County Public Schools, nearly 85 percent of 8th graders take or already have completed Algebra I, helping to meet our goal that every student has access to high-quality academic programming.
If schools aren't geeking about math, who will?
